what_this_is: Hand-written answer fixtures for the citation faithfulness harness (2D.1c). There is no model in 2D.1 — no API key — so these stand in for what one would emit. They are NOT a sample of real model output and must never be quoted as a measurement of the model.
why_broken_ones: R2: a guard that never refused is untested. A fixture of only well-formed answers would exercise the happy path and prove nothing about whether the harness can SEE a bad citation. Each entry names the count it is built to trigger, so a harness change that stops detecting one fails loudly instead of quietly reporting zeros.
the_important_case: `a04` is the one that matters. It is fluent, it is factually true, its marker is a real passage number, and the passage it names does not state the claim. Nothing about it looks wrong to a reader who does not open the citation.
why_passages_are_explicit: Each entry lists the chunk ids behind markers [1], [2], ... instead of taking whatever retrieval ranked first. Ranking is embedder-dependent, so a fixture that relied on it would silently stop testing what it claims to test the moment the embedder changed — a04 would start citing the right chunk and count 2 would quietly go to zero. Retrieval quality is measured separately, by the floor sweep.

answers.why: Faithful baseline. Every claim ends in a marker and the marker names the passage that states it.
answers.text: The pupil is the hole at the center of the eye that allows light to enter [1]. The iris is a smooth muscle that opens or closes it [1].

answers.why: Faithful baseline over a longer, more technical passage.
answers.text: The rod-shaped outer segments of the rod photoreceptor contain a stack of membrane-bound discs holding the photosensitive pigment rhodopsin [1]. Cones hold their photosensitive pigments in infoldings of the cell membrane instead [1].

answers.why: Count 1. Marker [9] names a passage that was never in the prompt. Pure invention, and the cheapest failure to detect. It also registers in count 2, because the sentence ends up resting on nothing — the two counts measure markers wrong and sentences wrong, and one bad marker can be both.
answers.text: Visual acuity is greatest at the fovea, where the retina lacks supporting cells and blood vessels [9].

answers.why: Count 2, THE case. Every word of this is true and the chapter does say it — in passage [2]. The marker points at [1], which is about photoreceptors. Fluent, correct, wrongly cited, and invisible to anyone who does not open the citation.
answers.text: The choroid is a layer of highly vascularized connective tissue that provides the blood supply to the eyeball [1].

answers.why: Count 3. The sclera is named in passage [1]; its thickness is not stated there or anywhere else. A confident number with no chunk behind it is fabrication, not a missing marker.
answers.text: The sclera is roughly 0.5 millimetres thick at the equator of the eye and thickens to about 1 millimetre near the optic nerve.

answers.why: The Rule 6 refusal. It must score zero on all three counts: refusing is the designed behaviour, and a harness that counted it as an uncited claim would punish the one thing this system exists to do. The second sentence is a claim about the passages rather than about the world, which is the case the refusal detector has to get right.
answers.text: Your chapter does not cover retinal detachment. The passages describe the structure of the retina but say nothing about its causes or treatment.

answers.why: Not count 3. The first sentence is true and sits in passage [1]; it simply carries no marker. A formatting failure, and folding it into count 3 would make a prompt fix look like a grounding fix.
answers.text: The eye has three layers of tissue. The outermost is the fibrous tunic, which includes the sclera and the cornea [1].

answers.why: Faithful, and cites an OCR chunk. Used to check that the citation the student is shown is not presented identically to a digital one, and that the answer's confidence says so too (2D.1e, D-044).
answers.text: The posterior cavity is the space behind the lens, and it is filled with a more viscous fluid called the vitreous humor [1].
